newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines trade gap up sharply for nine months.
newsitem.headline: Philippines trade gap up sharply for nine months.

text.p: The Philippines' trade deficit widened sharply in the first nine months of 1996, the government said on Friday, but economists said the expansion was expected and not a cause of worry for the economy.

The National Statistics Office said the country's merchandise trade deficit expanded by 42.5 percent to $9.132 billion in the first nine months of the year compared with a deficit of $6.408 billion in the same period last year.
The figures were in line with economists' expectations that the gap would reach a record of more than $12 billion for the full year versus $9.091 billion in 1995, economists said.
"Overall, the trade deficit will still be manageable," said Lito Dalit, an economist of AsianBank Corp.
Dalit and other economists said the growth in the trade gap was expected as the economy expanded and more capital goods were imported.
The statistics office said imports of four aircraft in September contributed to the surge. The four aircraft cost a total of $271.8 million.
Imports expanded by 25 percent to $24.059 billion from $19.210 billion in the January to September period, while exports rose by 16.6 percent to $14.926 billion from $12.802 billion.

Gross national product (GNP) growth for 1996 is estimated at 7.0 percent in 1996 from 5.7 percent last year, a big jump from the stagnant years before President Fidel Ramos' government launched an economic reform programme in 1992.
The wider trade deficit has so far had little impact on inflation as the peso has weakened only slightly to an estimated average of 26.21 pesos for 1996 to the dollar versus 25.714 pesos.
The Philippine currency's strength came from strong inflows for direct and portfolio investments, foreign loans and remittances from overseas contract workers, economists said.
Inflation has averaged 9.1 percent for the January to October period versus 9.7 percent in the same period last year.
"There's a consensus building we should expect a depreciation of the peso next year. But that depends on the extent of dollar inflows," said Jose Cuyegkeng, research head of ING Barings Securities.

A possible credit upgrade next year from international credit rating agencies and the expected passage of an important tax reform bill should further boost investor confidence in the country and bring more dollar inflows, he said.

AsianBank's Dalit said helping to keep the deficit manageable was an expected rise in remittances from overseas workers next year by 14 percent to $8.0 billion from an estimate of $7 billion this year. In 1995, remittances reached $4.9 billion.

Analysts estimated the country's trade deficit would rise further to $13.5 billion to $14 billion next year but it was not alarming as the bulk of imports were used to purchase capital equipment for the expansion of the economy.
